proof.text: First establish the finite cube attachment used below. For any nonempty finite set $J$, write $P(J)$ for its subsets ordered by inclusion and $P_-(J)=P(J)\setminus\{J\}$. Choose $j\in J$ and put $I=J\setminus\{j\}$. The poset isomorphism $P(J)\cong[1]\times P(I)$ sends $K$ to $(\mathbf1_{j\in K},K\cap I)$. By the nerve definition, nerves of product posets are degreewise products and $N([1])=\Delta^1$. A weakly increasing flag in $P(J)$ avoids $J$ exactly when either every term omits $j$, or every intersection with $I$ is proper: if any term contains $j$, the final term contains $j$; avoiding $J$ then makes its intersection with $I$ proper, and every earlier intersection is contained in that proper intersection. Thus $N(P_-(J))$ is the union of $\{0\}\times N(P(I))$ and $\Delta^1\times N(P_-(I))$, with intersection $\{0\}\times N(P_-(I))$. This is their degreewise pushout. The inclusion into $\Delta^1\times N(P(I))$, after interchanging product coordinates, is the pushout-product of the degreewise-injective $N(P_-(I))\hookrightarrow N(P(I))$ and $\{0\}\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$. The latter is the horn $\Lambda_0^1$ and hence anodyne directly from the definition. The pushout-product theorem makes $N(P_-(J))\hookrightarrow N(P(J))$ anodyne. No induction or assumption $I\ne\varnothing$ is used: for $I=\varnothing$, $P_-(I)$ is the empty poset, whose nerve is empty.

source.place: Lemma 3.3.5.9 (00Z9), expanded coordinate calculation of its pushout-product

proof.text: Fix $n\geq1$ and $0\leq k\leq n$. Put $V=[n]$, $J=V\setminus\{k\}$ and $C=P_+(V)=P(V)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$. Here $J$ is nonempty. A nonempty subset of $V$ is a face of $\Lambda_k^n$ precisely when it omits some vertex other than $k$; the only nonempty subsets that fail this condition are $J$ and $V$. Apply the finite-complex formula and its compatibility with inclusions in the subdivision face-poset calculus, using the finite ordered poset $[n]$. It identifies $\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n$ with $N(C)$ and $\operatorname{Sd}\Lambda_k^n$ with $A=N(C\setminus\{J,V\})$, with the subdivided horn map the inclusion. All following unions and intersections mean simplicial subsets, computed as sets of flags in each degree.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.3 (00Z3), horn face-poset identification using Proposition 3.3.3.17 (00YL)

proof.text: Let $g:P(J)\to C$ be $T\mapsto T\cup\{k\}$ and let $G=N(g)(N(P(J)))$. The map $g$ is an order embedding, so $G$ consists exactly of flags all of whose terms contain $k$. A flag in $G$ cannot contain $J$; it belongs to $A$ exactly when it does not contain $V$, which under $g$ means avoiding the terminal subset $J$ of $P(J)$. Consequently $G\cap A=N(g)(N(P_-(J)))$. Set $Z=A\cup G$. Degreewise union along intersection gives the pushout square with upper row $N(P_-(J))\to A$ and lower row $N(P(J))\to Z$. Step 1 makes its left vertical map anodyne. Apply lifting-class closure under pushouts with $T$ the class of Kan fibrations to conclude that $A\hookrightarrow Z$ is anodyne.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.3 (00Z3), first pushout; its intersection calculation and pushout closure

proof.text:
Write $P_+(J)=P(J)\setminus\{\varnothing\}$ and $P_{\pm}(J)=P(J)\setminus\{\varnothing,J\}$. Define $h:[1]\times P_+(J)\to C$ by $h(0,T)=T$ and $h(1,T)=T\cup\{k\}$. This is an order embedding onto the induced subposet $C\setminus\{\{k\}\}$: the two sides distinguish whether $k$ is present, and a cross inequality from side $0$ to side $1$ says exactly $T\subseteq T'$, while the reverse cross inequality is impossible. Put $H=N(C\setminus\{\{k\}\})\cong\Delta^1\times N(P_+(J))$. We claim $Z\cup H=N(C)$. Indeed, a flag outside $H$ contains $\{k\}$, so all its terms contain $k$ and it lies in $G\subseteq Z$. In a flag in $H$, membership in $G$ says that every side coordinate equals $1$. If some side coordinate is $0$, the flag is outside $G$ and is in $A$ exactly when no underlying $T$ is $J$: a side-$0$ term with $T=J$ is the excluded vertex $J$, and a side-$1$ such term is the excluded vertex $V$. Thus the preimage of $Z\cap H$ is exactly
$$D=(\{1\}\times N(P_+(J)))\amalg_{\{1\}\times N(P_{\pm}(J))}(\Delta^1\times N(P_{\pm}(J))).$$
These statements hold for weak flags, hence in every simplicial degree and compatibly with all operators. Since the two embedded subsets cover $N(C)$ and intersect as calculated, the square with top row $D\to Z$ and bottom row $\Delta^1\times N(P_+(J))\to N(C)$ is a degreewise pushout.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.3 (00Z3), second pushout, with full cover and intersection verification

proof.text: The map $D\hookrightarrow\Delta^1\times N(P_+(J))$ is, after swapping product coordinates, the pushout-product of the monomorphism $N(P_{\pm}(J))\hookrightarrow N(P_+(J))$ and the endpoint inclusion $\{1\}\hookrightarrow\Delta^1$. This endpoint inclusion is the horn $\Lambda_1^1$, hence anodyne by definition. Apply the pushout-product theorem and then lifting-class pushout closure to the second square in step 4. It follows that $Z\hookrightarrow N(C)$ is anodyne. Lifting-class closure under binary composition combines it with step 3 to give the anodyne map $A\hookrightarrow N(C)$. By step 2 this is $\operatorname{Sd}(\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n)$. This establishes subdivided horn lifting for every positive $n$ and every $k$, including both outer horns.

source.place: Proposition 3.3.5.3 (00Z3), pushout-product and composition after the second pushout

proof.text: Use the natural Hom bijection of the subdivision face-poset calculus to pass from horns to arbitrary maps without invoking weak saturation. Let $p:E\to B$ be any Kan fibration. For a square with left side $\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$ and right side $\operatorname{Ex}(p)$, denote its horizontal maps by $a:\Lambda_k^n\to\operatorname{Ex}E$ and $b:\Delta^n\to\operatorname{Ex}B$. Their adjoints $\widetilde a:\operatorname{Sd}\Lambda_k^n\to E$ and $\widetilde b:\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to B$ satisfy $p\widetilde a=\widetilde b\operatorname{Sd}(\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n)$ by both naturality identities of that bijection. Step 5 says that the left side of this transposed square is anodyne, so its lifting property against $p$ supplies $t:\operatorname{Sd}\Delta^n\to E$. Its transpose fills the original square, again by naturality and injectivity of the Hom bijection. Hence $\operatorname{Ex}(p)$ is a Kan fibration. This argument uses only the proved subdivided horn case, not subdivision preservation for general anodyne maps.

source.place: Agent-expanded lifting-square form of the horn reduction in 00Z3, using the Sd–Ex adjunction of Corollary 3.3.3.4

proof.text: Finally let $f:X\to Y$ be anodyne and let $p:E\to B$ be any Kan fibration. In any square with left side $\operatorname{Sd}(f)$ and right side $p$, write the horizontal maps as $u:\operatorname{Sd}X\to E$ and $v:\operatorname{Sd}Y\to B$. Their adjoints satisfy $\operatorname{Ex}(p)u^{\sharp}=v^{\sharp}f$ by naturality. By step 6 the right side $\operatorname{Ex}(p)$ is a Kan fibration. The hypothesis on $f$ therefore supplies $s:Y\to\operatorname{Ex}E$ with $sf=u^{\sharp}$ and $\operatorname{Ex}(p)s=v^{\sharp}$. Transpose $s$ to $\widetilde s:\operatorname{Sd}Y\to E$. Naturality gives $\widetilde s\operatorname{Sd}(f)=u$ and $p\widetilde s=v$. This is the required filler for the original arbitrary square. Thus $\operatorname{Sd}(f)$ has the left lifting property against every Kan fibration, which is exactly the asserted anodyne property.

source.place: Agent-expanded adjunction reduction from the horn calculation of Proposition 3.3.5.3 (00Z3) to arbitrary anodyne maps

title: Subdivision preserves anodyne extensions
statement: Use small simplicial sets of [def-weil-pbc-simplicial-set] and the subdivision functor $\operatorname{Sd}$ of [lem-coef-subdivision-face-poset-calculus]. As in [lem-coef-sset-anodyne-pushout-product], a Kan fibration is a map having the right lifting property against every horn inclusion $\Lambda_k^n\hookrightarrow\Delta^n$, $n\geq1$, $0\leq k\leq n$, and a map is anodyne if it has the left lifting property against every Kan fibration. For every anodyne map $f:X\to Y$ of small simplicial sets, $\operatorname{Sd}(f):\operatorname{Sd}X\to\operatorname{Sd}Y$ is anodyne.
